title: The bread with no time to rise

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there a family story you’ve heard so many times it feels like your own memory?
options: then you’re ready for this night. listen.
then here’s a good one to borrow. listen.
then hold that wish. this story was made to be handed on.

steps.line: In the book of Exodus, the Israelites are slaves in Egypt. Their lives are made bitter with hard work, with mortar and bricks.
After ten plagues, Pharaoh finally lets them go. And they leave in a rush, that very night.

steps.q: They’re leaving so fast, with the bread dough not yet risen. How do they carry it?
o: In sacks, loaded on carts with the grain
Bowls tied in cloaks, on their shoulders
In baskets, slung across their donkeys
steps.why: Exodus says it: the kneading bowls bound up in their cloaks, on their shoulders. No time even to pack.

steps.line: They carry their dough before it can rise, the kneading bowls wrapped in their cloaks, up on their shoulders.
On the road, they bake it into flat cakes. There had been no time to wait. That flat bread is matzah.

steps.q: For the week of Passover, many Jewish families don’t only eat matzah. What else do they do?
o: Clear every bread crumb out of the house
Bake a fresh loaf for the first night
Skip all grains for the whole week
steps.why: Leavened food is called chametz. The night before, many families search the house by candlelight for the last crumbs, often with a feather and a wooden spoon.

steps.line: Every spring, at the Passover seder, Jewish families tell it again. Seder means order, and the plate lays the story out as food.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Match each food to what it recalls.
steps.why: You taste the story before anyone explains it. Plates differ a little from family to family.

steps.line: Then the youngest stands up and asks: “Why is this night different from all other nights?”
steps.label: today

steps.pre: The answer doesn’t begin “once upon a time.” It begins: “
steps.post: were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt.”
steps.why: We. Not they. An old teaching says that in every generation, each person should see themselves as if they walked out of Egypt.

say: here’s what i love. the first passover wasn’t calm or tidy. it was dough on your shoulder and no time to wait.
in jewish tradition, the seder isn’t a history lesson. it’s a memory you’re handed, so each person feels they left egypt too. families tell it in their own ways, with their own questions.

steps.q: The Torah says, “tell your child on that day.” So why is the telling built around a child’s question?
o: So the grown-ups can test what children know
A story sticks best when someone asks for it
steps.why: The night is built to make the young ask, and the old answer. That’s how a memory gets handed down.

today.say: this week, ask someone older one question about your own family’s story, and let them tell it. that’s the seder’s whole idea: memory is handed down by asking.
options: then ask. the telling is the gift.
There’s no one left to ask
then tell it yourself, to someone younger. that’s how it’s carried.

sources: Exodus 1:13–14 (bitter lives, with mortar and brick)
Exodus 12:31–34, 39 (sent out that night; dough taken before it was leavened, kneading bowls bound in their cloaks on their shoulders; baked into unleavened cakes)
Exodus 13:8 (you shall tell your child on that day)
Mishnah Pesachim 10:4–5 (the child asks; bitter herbs for the bitterness of slavery; in every generation a person must see himself as if he came out of Egypt)
Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 116a (charoset in memory of the mortar)
The Passover Haggadah (the four questions; avadim hayinu, we were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt)
